p: My family went to Korea for a holiday. We ate bibimbap and walked around a palace. My grandma showed me her old school.
Japan is a country with many islands. People there eat sushi and ramen. In spring, pink cherry blossoms cover the trees.
In China, pandas live in bamboo forests. They eat bamboo for most of the day. Pandas are black and white.
We have a big map in our classroom. We put a pin on every country our families come from. There are pins all over the map.
To go overseas, you need a passport. It has your photo and your name. A stamp goes in it when you visit a new country.
New Zealand is near Australia. It has big mountains and green hills. The Maori people have their own language and culture.

s: Indonesia is Australia's nearest large neighbour and is made up of thousands of islands.
The Korean alphabet, called Hangul, was created by King Sejong in the fifteenth century.
Chinese New Year is also called the Spring Festival.
The Mekong River flows through six countries in South-East Asia.
Japan has trains called shinkansen that can travel over three hundred kilometres an hour.
India has more than twenty official languages.
Many Pacific Island nations are threatened by rising sea levels.
The Great Wall of China was built over many centuries to protect the empire.
Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights celebrated with lamps and sweets.
Trade between Australia and Asia includes iron ore, wheat and education.
Vietnam is famous for pho, a noodle soup with fresh herbs.
The Philippines has more than seven thousand islands.
K-pop music and Korean dramas are popular all over the world.
Mount Everest, the highest mountain, is on the border of Nepal and China.
Many students from Asia come to study at Australian universities.
Papua New Guinea is Australia's closest neighbour to the north.
Rice is the main food for billions of people in Asia.
Ramadan is a month when many Muslims fast from sunrise to sunset.
Singapore is a small island country with one of the busiest ports in the world.
Learning a second language helps you understand another culture.
The Silk Road was an ancient trade route between China and Europe.
Thailand has never been colonised by a European power.
Malaysia's Petronas Towers were once the tallest buildings in the world.
Time zones mean it can be night in Australia while it is day in Europe.
Kindness is understood in every language.
p: Australia is located in the Asia-Pacific region, and many of our closest neighbours are Asian countries. Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and New Zealand are all nearby. Australia trades, travels and studies with these countries, and many Australians have family connections to Asia.

Lunar New Year is celebrated in many countries, including China, Korea and Vietnam. Families gather for special meals, give red envelopes with money to children and wear new clothes. In Korea the holiday is called Seollal, and people bow to their elders to show respect. Australian cities hold parades with dragon and lion dances.

Korea is a peninsula in East Asia. Its capital, Seoul, is a busy modern city filled with tall buildings, palaces and markets. Korean food such as kimchi and bulgogi is enjoyed around the world. The Korean alphabet, Hangul, is known for being simple and easy to learn.

Japan is an island nation in the Pacific Ocean. It is famous for its technology, fast trains and traditional culture. Many Japanese people celebrate the cherry blossom season by having picnics under the trees. Students in Japan often help clean their classrooms at the end of the day.

The Pacific Islands include countries such as Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and Vanuatu. Many islands are low-lying, which means rising sea levels caused by climate change are a serious threat. Pacific Islanders have a strong connection to the ocean and are famous for their navigation skills.

Learning another language opens up new ways of thinking and new friendships. In Australia, students may learn Japanese, Indonesian, Chinese, Korean, French or Italian. Knowing even a few words, like hello and thank you, shows respect when you visit another country.

s: Australia's economy is closely linked to Asia, which buys a large share of its exports.
Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country and one of the biggest democracies.
The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice, but no formal peace treaty was ever signed.
Rapid urbanisation in Asia has created some of the largest cities the world has ever seen.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations promotes cooperation and stability in the region.
Cultural exchange programs allow students to live with host families and study overseas.
Pacific nations are leading voices in international negotiations on climate change.
The Colombo Plan brought thousands of Asian students to study in Australia from the 1950s.
Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world, which creates economic challenges.
India's space agency has successfully landed a spacecraft near the moon's south pole.
Globalisation means products, ideas and people move more freely around the world.
Learning Asian languages can open doors to careers in business, diplomacy and tourism.
Many Australian cities have twin-city relationships with cities in Asia.
Monsoon rains are essential for farming in South and South-East Asia.
South Korea transformed from a poor nation into a technology powerhouse in only a few decades.
Foreign aid supports health, education and disaster relief in developing countries.
Respecting cultural customs, such as removing shoes indoors, is important when travelling.
The Belt and Road Initiative is a major infrastructure program led by China.
Timor-Leste became an independent nation in 2002 after a long struggle.
Refugees are people who have fled their countries because of war or persecution.
The United Nations was founded in 1945 to promote peace and international cooperation.
Fair trade products aim to ensure farmers in developing countries receive fair prices.
Tourism brings income to many Asian countries but can also strain local environments.
Australia participates in regional forums to discuss security, trade and the environment.
Understanding other perspectives helps us become thoughtful global citizens.
p: Australia's relationship with Asia has grown stronger over recent decades. Countries such as China, Japan, South Korea and India are among Australia's largest trading partners, buying resources, food and education services. Millions of Australians have Asian heritage, and Asian languages are widely spoken across the country. Understanding the history and cultures of the region is increasingly important for young Australians.

South Korea has undergone one of the fastest economic transformations in history. After the Korean War, it was one of the poorest countries in the world. Through investment in education, manufacturing and technology, it became a leading producer of cars, ships, smartphones and semiconductors. Today Korean culture, from music to film, is popular around the world.

The Pacific Islands are home to diverse cultures with deep connections to the ocean. Many island nations face serious threats from rising sea levels, stronger cyclones and coastal erosion. Leaders from countries such as Tuvalu and Kiribati have urged the world to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Australia works with Pacific neighbours on climate adaptation, health and security.

Indonesia, Australia's closest large neighbour, is a nation of more than seventeen thousand islands and over two hundred and seventy million people. It has hundreds of ethnic groups and languages, united by the national language, Bahasa Indonesia. Bali is a popular destination for Australian tourists, but Indonesia's culture and economy extend far beyond its beaches.

Globalisation describes the increasing connection between countries through trade, travel, communication and culture. It has helped lift many people out of poverty and made a huge range of goods available. However, it has also been criticised for widening inequality, harming local industries and spreading environmental damage. Balancing these benefits and costs is a major challenge for governments.

Refugees are people forced to leave their homes because of war, violence or persecution. Many spend years in camps before they can be resettled in a new country. Australia has accepted refugees from many parts of the world, including Vietnam, Afghanistan, Syria and South Sudan. Settlement services help new arrivals learn English, find work and build new lives.

s: The Indo-Pacific has become the centre of global economic growth and strategic competition in the twenty-first century.
Australia's foreign policy must balance its security alliance with the United States and its trade relationship with China.
Soft power, including culture, education and diplomacy, allows nations to influence others without coercion.
The rise of the Korean Wave demonstrates how popular culture can shape a country's international image.
Regional institutions such as ASEAN play a crucial role in managing tensions and fostering cooperation.
Climate change is increasingly framed as a security threat, particularly for low-lying Pacific nations.
Global supply chains proved vulnerable during the pandemic, prompting countries to reconsider their reliance on imports.
International education is one of Australia's largest service exports, connecting students across the region.
Development aid is most effective when it is designed in partnership with local communities.
The demographic dividend describes economic growth that can occur when a country's working-age population increases.
Cultural intelligence, the ability to work effectively across cultures, is highly valued by employers.
Disputes in the South China Sea involve competing territorial claims and important shipping routes.
Diaspora communities maintain strong ties with their countries of origin through family, business and culture.
Free trade agreements reduce tariffs but can also raise concerns about labour standards and sovereignty.
The reunification of Korea remains an aspiration for many, though political obstacles remain immense.
Middle powers like Australia can exert influence by building coalitions and supporting international law.
Rapid economic growth in Asia has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty.
Language learning in Australian schools has declined, despite repeated calls to build Asia literacy.
Global health security depends on cooperation in surveillance, research and vaccine distribution.
Tourism can promote cross-cultural understanding but may also commodify local traditions.
Human rights diplomacy requires balancing principled advocacy with practical engagement.
Pacific regionalism emphasises shared ocean identity and collective responses to common challenges.
Technological competition, especially in semiconductors and artificial intelligence, shapes modern geopolitics.
Migration flows reflect economic opportunity, conflict, environmental pressures and family connections.
Global citizenship involves recognising our responsibilities to people beyond national borders.
p: Australia occupies a distinctive position in the Indo-Pacific. Its closest security partner is the United States, while its largest trading partner for many years has been China. Managing these relationships requires careful diplomacy, particularly when strategic competition between the two powers intensifies. Many analysts argue that Australia should strengthen ties with a broad range of regional partners, including Indonesia, India, Japan and the Pacific nations, to reduce dependence on any single relationship.

The Korean Wave, or Hallyu, refers to the global spread of South Korean popular culture, including music, television dramas, films, food and beauty products. Government support, sophisticated marketing and the rise of social media helped Korean content reach audiences worldwide. The phenomenon has boosted tourism and exports and enhanced South Korea's international reputation, illustrating how soft power can complement economic and diplomatic strategies.

Pacific Island nations have long argued that climate change is the single greatest threat to their security and wellbeing. Rising sea levels threaten freshwater supplies, agriculture and, in some cases, the habitability of entire islands. Leaders have used international forums to call for more ambitious emission cuts and financial support for adaptation. These debates raise profound questions about sovereignty, migration and responsibility for historical emissions.

Asia literacy refers to knowledge and understanding of the histories, cultures, languages and economies of Asian countries. Successive Australian governments have emphasised its importance, given the region's economic and strategic significance. Yet the proportion of students studying Asian languages in senior years remains relatively low. Advocates argue that greater investment in teacher training, exchange programs and early language learning is needed to prepare young Australians for a regional future.

Global supply chains allow products to be designed in one country, manufactured in another and sold around the world. This system has lowered costs and increased efficiency, but the pandemic exposed its fragility when shortages of medicines, semiconductors and other essential goods disrupted economies. Many governments are now pursuing supply chain resilience, encouraging diversification and domestic production of critical items, even at higher cost.

Effective international development requires more than financial assistance. Projects that are designed without local input often fail to meet community needs or are abandoned when funding ends. Increasingly, aid organisations emphasise partnership, local leadership and long-term capacity building. Evaluating outcomes rigorously and listening to the people affected are essential to ensuring that development programs deliver lasting improvements in health, education and livelihoods.
